deep.reconstruction:
This page has no mathematics: no formulas, derivations or computations. It is methodological prose continuing the introduction of Riemann's essay on the mechanics of the ear. The essay was published posthumously by Henle in 1867 as "Mechanik des Ohres" (Zeitschrift für rationelle Medicin, 3. Reihe, Bd. 29) and is reprinted in Riemann's Gesammelte Werke.

The page's content:
(1) It completes the sentence begun on fol. 12r (p. 7). The performances (Leistungen) of the hearing organ must be established by observation and experiment as precisely as possible. These include the sharpness, fineness and fidelity with which the ear conveys sound, its timbre (Klang) and pitch (Ton), its intensity and its direction.
(2) Riemann takes these facts as known. He refers the reader to Helmholtz's book 'Die Lehre von den Tonempfindungen als physiologische Grundlage für die Theorie der Musik' (1st ed. 1863). That book collects the recent progress in establishing the facts of tone perception, made mainly by Helmholtz himself.
(3) He says he must often oppose the conclusions Helmholtz draws from his experiments and observations. He therefore acknowledges at the outset the great merits of Helmholtz's work. In his view these merits lie not in Helmholtz's theory of the motions of the ear, but in improving the empirical basis for a theory of those motions.

This frames Riemann's later critique of the Helmholtz resonance picture. That critique concerns the role of the ossicles and tympanic membrane as a faithful transmitting apparatus, and the cochlea. Its mathematical content (small-amplitude mechanics of the ossicular chain, fidelity of transmission) appears on later folios, not here. The next page (p. 9) cites Henle's Handbuch der Anatomie, Bd. 2, 3. Lieferung (1866). Together with this page, that dates the manuscript to Riemann's last year, 1866.

results.what: Methodological statement: take the ear's empirically established performances (as collected by Helmholtz 1863) as given. Accept Helmholtz's empirical results but reject his theory of the ear's motions.
results.modern_name: Riemann's critique of Helmholtz's theory of hearing (prefatory remarks of 'Mechanik des Ohres')
results.usually_credited_to: Bernhard Riemann, 'Mechanik des Ohres', published posthumously by J. Henle, 1867

deep.surprise_reason: This is purely prose. It is the published introduction of Riemann's well-known posthumous essay 'Mechanik des Ohres' (1867, in the Werke), whose critique of Helmholtz is documented in the literature. The page contains no mathematics.
